title: Solvara launch — market access & prior authorization workflow design
client: Veloxa Therapeutics, Inc. — a US specialty pharmaceutical company (~$900M revenue) preparing the first commercial launch of a product it owns. The product is Solvara (velankibart), a subcutaneous, self-administered biologic for the maintenance treatment of generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP), a rare and severe dermatologic condition. PDUFA approval is expected in Q4 2026; launch planning is underway as of June 2026. Veloxa has never operated a specialty-drug market-access or patient-support infrastructure of its own.
consultant_role: Principal at Copeland Access Partners, a US market-access consultancy, engaged by Veloxa's VP of Market Access to design (a) the US market access strategy and (b) the end-to-end prior-authorization workflow for the Solvara launch. The engagement partner is Elaine Voss, author of the Copeland engagement standards that govern deliverable style.

cast.name: Marcus Feld
cast.role: VP Market Access, Veloxa Therapeutics (client sponsor)
cast.reliability_note: Commercially candid, sponsors the engagement because Veloxa has no in-house access machinery. Defers on operational detail; occasionally repeats optimistic launch-deck framing (e.g. the 12,000-patient headline) without owning the number.

cast.name: Aaron Deng
cast.reliability_note: CONFIDENTLY WRONG JUNIOR VOICE. His access memo plans Solvara as a buy-and-bill product billed under Medicare Part B (wrong — subcutaneous self-administered biologics run on the pharmacy benefit / Part D) and proposes offering the manufacturer copay card to all patients including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries (illegal under the federal Anti-Kickback Statute). Fluent and specific; never adopt his recommendations without corroboration.

cast.name: Dr. Nadia Okoro
cast.reliability_note: AUTHORITATIVE EXPERT VOICE. Sits on the health plan side. In the advisory-board transcript she pins the realistic candidate fraction (~55% of diagnosed GPP), the realistic first-pass PA approval bands, why step therapy is inappropriate for acute GPP presentation, and reminds the room that copay cards cannot be used by government-insured patients. Trust her judgment; her figures anchor the triangulations.

cast.name: Elaine Voss
cast.reliability_note: Author of the Copeland engagement standards (house style). Reliable and precise on deliverable conventions and on the evidence hierarchy (system data and executed policy over decks and marketing). Her standards doc governs both deliverables.

cast.name: Sofia Marchetti
cast.reliability_note: Owns the gross-to-net pricing memo. Accurate on WAC ($150,000/patient-year), blended gross-to-net erosion (~42%), the Medicaid statutory rebate floor (23.1%), and 340B exposure. Authoritative for pricing figures; the launch deck's rosier net assumptions are not hers.

cast.name: Daniel Roth
cast.role: Associate General Counsel — Healthcare Compliance, Veloxa
cast.reliability_note: AUTHORITATIVE on legal constraints. His compliance email is the binding word that copay assistance may not be offered to Medicare/Medicaid/TRICARE beneficiaries (Anti-Kickback Statute / beneficiary-inducement), and flags copay accumulator/maximizer exposure. Directly refutes Aaron Deng's copay-to-all proposal.

cast.name: Tanya Brooks
cast.reliability_note: Source of field intelligence. Her email thread reports what plans verbally quote for PA turnaround (one plan quotes '15 business days'), which conflicts with binding state PA-turnaround statutes. Accurate reporter of what she hears; the quoted SLA is not the governing number.

cast.name: Greg Halloran
cast.reliability_note: Designs the hub. His email thread pins the bridge (free trial) program at up to 30 days / two fills and the commercial copay program at a $20,000 annual maximum. Reliable on hub operational design; his numbers override the launch deck's '90-day bridge'.

cast.name: Renu Iyer
cast.reliability_note: Owns the launch-readiness tracker and the internal launch-strategy deck v3. The deck aggregates optimistic planning figures (12,000 addressable patients, 70% commercial mix, 80% first-pass approval, open distribution across 15 specialty pharmacies, 90-day bridge) that later evidence corrects. She is organized, not a domain authority; the deck is a planning artifact, not evidence.

cast.name: James Whitfield
cast.role: Senior Consultant, Copeland Access Partners (reliable peer)
cast.reliability_note: Solid analyst on the engagement. In Slack he pushes back on the deck's payer-mix and approval numbers, points to the claims extract and coverage matrix as the real sources, and flags Aaron Deng's buy-and-bill and copay errors. Trustworthy.

cast.name: Dr. Priya Anand
cast.role: Epidemiologist, author of the commissioned GPP epidemiology report
cast.reliability_note: Authoritative for disease prevalence: US diagnosed prevalent GPP ~7,500 patients, with the age distribution that drives the Medicare share. Careful about the diagnosed-vs-addressable distinction and the L40.1 vs L40.0 ICD-10 coding ambiguity. Her diagnosed count is not the addressable count.

product_generic_name.note: Solvara is the brand; velankibart the (fictional) nonproprietary name. Subcutaneous, self-administered biologic for maintenance treatment of GPP.

benefit_type.value: pharmacy benefit (Medicare via Part D), not medical benefit / buy-and-bill under Part B
benefit_type.note: Because Solvara is subcutaneous and self-administered at home, it adjudicates on the pharmacy benefit; Medicare coverage is via Part D, not Part B buy-and-bill. Aaron Deng's memo plans Part B buy-and-bill — the central benefit-design trap.

us_diagnosed_gpp.note: US diagnosed prevalent GPP population per the epidemiology report (range 6,800-8,200). This is the DIAGNOSED count, not the addressable/candidate count. The launch deck misuses it (and inflates further to 12,000).

candidate_fraction.note: Share of diagnosed GPP patients who are realistic candidates for a new subcutaneous maintenance biologic (comorbidities, prior therapy, acute-vs-maintenance status). Dr. Okoro pins 'a bit over half, call it 55%'; the claims extract corroborates (~54% of GPP-coded patients carry a systemic/biologic claim).

us_addressable_patients.note: 7,500 diagnosed x 0.55 candidate fraction = ~4,125. Recovered ONLY by triangulating epidemiology (diagnosed count), the claims extract (treated fraction), and the advisory board (candidate fraction). No single source states it. Traps: 7,500 (diagnosed) and 12,000 (deck inflation).
us_addressable_patients.authoritative_source: answer key (derived from epi report + claims extract + advisory board)

commercial_share_pct.units: fraction of insured lives on therapy
commercial_share_pct.note: Commercial payer share of the treated GPP population. Claims extract summary shows ~55% commercial; epi age distribution (skew toward working-age adults) supports it; advisory board confirms. Deck says 70% (trap).

medicare_partd_share_pct.note: Medicare (Part D) share ~22%, driven by the older tail of the GPP age distribution. Runs on the pharmacy benefit under Part D, not Part B.

medicaid_share_pct.note: Medicaid share ~18% (fee-for-service + managed Medicaid). Heaviest step-therapy and PA burden; lowest first-pass approval.

uninsured_share_pct.note: Uninsured/other ~5%. Routed to the Patient Assistance Program (free drug), NOT to PA or the commercial copay program.

commercial_first_pass_pct.note: Expected first-pass PA approval on commercial plans, from the analog coverage matrix and advisory board.

medicare_first_pass_pct.note: Expected first-pass Part D coverage-determination approval.

medicaid_first_pass_pct.note: Expected first-pass Medicaid approval; step-therapy heavy.

blended_first_pass_pct.note: Share-weighted first-pass approval across insured segments: (0.55*0.62 + 0.22*0.55 + 0.18*0.40)/0.95 = 0.534/0.95 = 0.562 ~ 56%. Triangulates segment shares (claims/epi) x per-segment rates (coverage matrix/advisory). Deck claims 80% (trap); analog biologic B shows 70% for an established product (trap).
blended_first_pass_pct.authoritative_source: answer key (derived from payer_coverage_matrix.csv + gpp_claims_extract_2025.csv + advisory board)

annual_wac_usd.note: Solvara planned WAC (list) is $150,000/patient-year, pinned identically in the product profile and pricing memo. The analog biologic B policy references $180,000 for a DIFFERENT product (trap).

blended_gross_to_net_pct.note: Blended gross-to-net erosion ~42% across the payer mix (commercial rebates, Medicaid statutory rebate + inflation penalty, 340B, copay assistance). Net ~ $150,000 x 0.58 = ~$87,000/patient-year.

medicaid_statutory_rebate_pct.note: Statutory Medicaid rebate floor for a single-source innovator biologic is 23.1% of AMP, before the CPI-based inflation penalty. A domain constant Veloxa cannot negotiate away.

sp_network_size.note: Solvara launches through a LIMITED distribution network of 4 specialty pharmacies (selected=Y in the network options file). The deck's 'open distribution / 15 SPs' is the trap.

bridge_program_days.note: Free-drug bridge for patients with a pending PA: up to 30 days / two fills, per the hub-vendor design thread. The deck's '90-day bridge' is unfunded and out of line with hub economics (trap).

copay_program_annual_max_usd.note: Commercial copay program: $0 patient cost up to a $20,000 annual maximum. COMMERCIAL PLANS ONLY. Government beneficiaries (Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE) are legally excluded.

copay_government_exclusion.value: prohibited for federal healthcare program beneficiaries
copay_government_exclusion.note: Manufacturer copay cards cannot be offered to Medicare/Medicaid/TRICARE patients under the federal Anti-Kickback Statute and beneficiary-inducement rules. Government-insured patients unable to afford therapy are routed to an independent charitable foundation or the PAP, never the copay card. Aaron Deng's copay-to-all plan is illegal.

state_statute_standard_turnaround_days.note: Binding state PA-turnaround statutes cap standard determinations at 7 calendar days and expedited/urgent at 72 hours. These floors override any longer plan-quoted SLA (one plan verbally quotes '15 business days' — not lawful for covered lives in statute states).

step_therapy_gpp_position.value: step-therapy exception path required; step therapy inappropriate for acute GPP
step_therapy_gpp_position.note: Analog coverage policy A requires step through two systemics; GPP acute flares are life-threatening and the label + advisory board support bypassing step therapy via a documented exception. The workflow must build a step-therapy exception path rather than accept the step requirement.

icd10_gpp_code.note: Generalized pustular psoriasis codes to ICD-10 L40.1. Miscoding to L40.0 (psoriasis vulgaris) is a common cause of PA denial; the workflow's benefits-verification step must confirm L40.1.

contradictions.topic: Benefit type: pharmacy benefit vs Part B buy-and-bill

claim_a.quote: Solvara should be set up as a buy-and-bill product: sites of care purchase and bill it under the medical benefit, with Medicare reimbursing under Part B via a J-code.

claim_b.quote: Solvara is a subcutaneous biologic self-administered by the patient at home; it adjudicates on the pharmacy benefit, and Medicare coverage is provided under Part D.

contradictions.resolution: Solvara runs on the pharmacy benefit. Because it is subcutaneous and self-administered, there is no in-office administration to buy-and-bill; Medicare coverage is under Part D, not Part B. The Part D coverage-determination brief confirms the pathway. The workflow must be a pharmacy-benefit / specialty-pharmacy workflow, and must not contain buy-and-bill or Part B billing steps.
contradictions.why_decidable: The product profile is the definitive statement of route of administration and site of care; a self-administered subcutaneous injectable cannot be buy-and-billed. The Medicare Part D brief independently confirms the Part D pathway. The junior memo cites no product-level basis.

claim_a.quote: We assume a commercially-favorable payer mix of roughly 70% commercial, with government payers a minority of demand.

claim_b.quote: primary_payer distribution across the GPP-coded cohort: Commercial 55%, Medicare 22%, Medicaid 18%, Uninsured 5%

contradictions.resolution: Commercial is ~55%, not 70%. The claims extract, the epidemiology age distribution, and the advisory board all land near 55% commercial with a material Medicare (22%) and Medicaid (18%) share. The 70% figure is an unsupported planning assumption.
contradictions.why_decidable: A claims-based payer distribution over the actual disease cohort beats a slide-level planning assumption with no cited basis; two independent sources (epi, advisory board) corroborate 55%.

claim_a.quote: Total addressable US GPP population of up to 12,000 patients represents the launch opportunity.

claim_b.quote: US diagnosed prevalent GPP is estimated at approximately 7,500 patients (range 6,800-8,200).

contradictions.resolution: The addressable population is ~4,125: 7,500 diagnosed x 55% candidate fraction. The deck's 12,000 inflates well beyond even the diagnosed count; 7,500 is the diagnosed number, not the addressable one. Only triangulating epi + claims + advisory yields the addressable figure.
contradictions.why_decidable: The epidemiology report is the authoritative disease-size source and explicitly bounds diagnosed prevalence below 8,200; the candidate haircut is set by the payer medical director and corroborated by the claims treated-fraction. 12,000 has no evidentiary basis.

claim_a.quote: We model an 80% first-pass prior-authorization approval rate at launch.

claim_b.quote: first_pass_approval_pct by segment: Commercial 62, Medicare Part D 55, Medicaid 40

contradictions.resolution: Blended first-pass is ~56% ((0.55x0.62 + 0.22x0.55 + 0.18x0.40)/0.95), not 80%. The 80% is a manufacturer-optimistic assumption. The advisory board explicitly says 'high 50s blended, not the 80s.'
contradictions.why_decidable: Segment-level approval rates from the analog coverage matrix, weighted by the claims-based payer mix, are a defensible bottom-up estimate; the deck's single 80% number is top-down with no support and is contradicted by the expert.

contradictions.topic: Copay assistance eligibility for government-insured patients

claim_a.quote: To minimize abandonment we should offer the $0 copay card to every patient, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, regardless of coverage.

claim_b.quote: Manufacturer copay assistance may not be offered to any federal healthcare program beneficiary — Medicare, Medicaid, or TRICARE — under the Anti-Kickback Statute and beneficiary-inducement rules. These patients are routed to an independent charitable foundation or the PAP, never the copay card.

contradictions.resolution: The copay program is COMMERCIAL-ONLY. Offering copay support to government beneficiaries is a federal felony risk. Government-insured patients who cannot afford therapy go to an independent charitable foundation or the free-drug PAP. The workflow and plan must reflect this exclusion; the junior recommendation must not appear.
contradictions.why_decidable: Associate General Counsel's compliance guidance states the binding legal constraint; it is not a matter of preference. The junior memo is legally wrong.

contradictions.topic: PA turnaround: plan-quoted SLA vs state statute

claim_a.quote: The plan's provider rep told me to expect about 15 business days for a standard PA determination on a new specialty product.

contradictions.resolution: State PA-turnaround statutes cap standard determinations at 7 calendar days and urgent at 72 hours. Where a statute applies, the plan's verbally-quoted 15 business days is not lawful and the statutory floor governs. The workflow SLAs and escalation logic must be built to the statute, treating 15 business days as a compliance escalation trigger, not the design target.
contradictions.why_decidable: A binding statute overrides a payer representative's informal quote. The statutes file states the enforceable maximum; the field intel is anecdotal reporting of a non-compliant practice.

claim_a.quote: Launch through open distribution across 15 specialty pharmacies to maximize access.

claim_b.quote: 12 candidate specialty pharmacies evaluated; selected = Y for exactly 4 (limited distribution network)

contradictions.resolution: Solvara launches through a LIMITED distribution network of 4 specialty pharmacies, not open distribution across 15. A rare, cold-chain, patient-support-intensive biologic requires a tightly managed network for data, adherence, and REMS-like oversight. The network options file records the 4 selected partners.
contradictions.why_decidable: The distribution decision is recorded in the network options file with explicit selection flags reflecting the launch team's actual decision; the deck's 15 is an early aspirational slide superseded by the selection.

claim_a.quote: A generous 90-day bridge program will keep patients on therapy while PAs are pending.

claim_b.quote: The bridge should be up to 30 days, two fills max, standard for a launch like this and what the budget supports.

contradictions.resolution: The bridge (free-drug) program is up to 30 days / two fills, not 90 days. The hub vendor and program budget support a 30-day bridge; a 90-day bridge is unfunded and out of line with launch norms. The workflow bridge-routing step uses 30 days.
contradictions.why_decidable: The hub vendor designing and pricing the program states the operational parameter; the deck's 90 days is an aspirational number with no funding basis.

claim_a.quote: Coverage requires documented trial and failure of at least two conventional systemic agents before a biologic will be authorized.

claim_b.quote: Step therapy through two systemics makes no clinical sense for an acute pustular flare — that patient can be in the hospital. The workflow has to lead with a step-therapy exception, not accept the step.

contradictions.resolution: GPP acute flares are severe and can be life-threatening; forcing step therapy through two systemics is clinically inappropriate. The workflow must build a step-therapy EXCEPTION path (label + guideline + acute-presentation documentation) rather than accept the analog policy's step requirement as a design constraint.
contradictions.why_decidable: The analog policy is a payer's generic biologic step rule not written for GPP; the payer medical director, speaking to GPP specifically and to how exceptions are actually adjudicated, is the authority for the design decision.

claim_a.quote: The reference biologic carries a wholesale acquisition cost of approximately $180,000 per patient per year.

claim_b.quote: Solvara planned WAC is $150,000 per patient per year.

contradictions.resolution: Solvara's planned WAC is $150,000/patient-year (confirmed identically in the product profile). The $180,000 figure belongs to a DIFFERENT analog biologic and must not be used as Solvara's price.
contradictions.why_decidable: Veloxa's own pricing memo and product profile state Solvara's WAC; the $180,000 is explicitly the reference (analog) product's price in a third-party coverage policy.

red_herrings.why_distracting: A polished internal launch deck aggregating optimistic planning numbers (12,000 addressable, 70% commercial, 80% first-pass, 15 open-distribution SPs, 90-day bridge). Reads like a finished strategy; importing its figures fails five contradictions at once. It is a planning artifact, not evidence.

Aaron Deng's confident, specific memo recommending Part B buy-and-bill and a copay card for all patients including Medicare/Medicaid. Both moves are wrong (one operationally, one illegal). Fluent and detailed — corroboration bait for a careless reader.

A real-looking coverage policy for a different, established analog biologic showing a 70% approval rate, a $180,000 WAC, and medical-benefit administration. Tempts the agent to lift the wrong price, the wrong approval rate, and a medical-benefit framing onto Solvara.

A dense internal RACI/milestone tracker full of mundane launch tasks and owners. Genuinely low-signal for the strategy and workflow, but tempting to mine for structure; it contains no authoritative access figures.

A detailed ICD-10 coding reference (L40.x family). Useful for the benefits-verification step's coding check, but a rabbit hole if over-weighted; the only load-bearing fact is L40.1 = GPP vs L40.0 miscode.

rules: Currency and units: all monetary figures in USD with a leading $ and thousands separators (e.g. $150,000); express approval rates, payer shares, and gross-to-net as percentages with a % sign. State per-patient figures on an annual basis ('per patient per year').
US spelling and ISO dates throughout (YYYY-MM-DD); spell out the benefit type (pharmacy benefit vs medical benefit) explicitly whenever a coverage pathway is named.

Source attribution: every quantitative claim in the strategy document must cite its source document inline in the exact format '(source: <filename>)', e.g. '(source: gpp_epidemiology_report_2026.md)'.

No recommendation-of-record language before the stated gate: the strategy must not present distribution, pricing, or copay design as final/approved; frame them as 'recommended, pending Veloxa legal and pricing-committee sign-off' until that gate. Use 'recommended', not 'approved' or 'final'.

Controlled vocabulary: benefit coverage pathway is one of exactly 'pharmacy benefit' or 'medical benefit'; PA outcomes are one of exactly 'approved', 'denied', or 'pended'; do not use ad-hoc synonyms in the workflow spec.

Compliance line: any patient-affordability mechanism must state its eligible population; copay assistance must be described as commercially-insured only, and no deliverable may describe offering copay assistance to a government-insured patient.

task.objective: Design (1) the US market access strategy and (2) the end-to-end prior-authorization workflow for the launch of Solvara (velankibart), a subcutaneous self-administered biologic for GPP, ahead of the expected Q4 2026 PDUFA approval. Ground every quantitative claim in the source pool, resolve the conflicts between the launch deck / junior memo and the underlying evidence, and respect the legal and statutory overlays (benefit-type routing, copay eligibility, PA-turnaround statutes).
requirements: Segment the US payer landscape (commercial, Medicare Part D, Medicaid, uninsured) with evidence-based shares, and specify the correct benefit-type routing for each — Solvara is a pharmacy-benefit product (Medicare via Part D), not a Part B buy-and-bill product.

Size the opportunity: report the diagnosed and the addressable GPP population, deriving the addressable figure by triangulating the epidemiology report, the claims extract, and the advisory board rather than adopting the launch deck's headline.

Design an end-to-end prior-authorization workflow covering intake, benefits verification (including ICD-10 L40.1 confirmation), PA preparation/submission, determination, denial and multi-level appeals, specialty-pharmacy fulfillment, bridge/PAP routing, and adherence follow-up, with realistic SLAs that honor state PA-turnaround statutes.

Design patient support (hub services, bridge program, copay program, PAP) that respects the legal constraint that copay assistance is for commercially-insured patients only and that government-insured patients are routed to an independent charitable foundation or the PAP.

State expected first-pass PA approval and gross-to-net economics using the source-anchored figures, not the launch deck's optimistic numbers; flag each place your analysis overrides the deck or the junior memo and say why.

Follow the Copeland Engagement Standards (sources/shared/reference/copeland_engagement_standards.md) for units, spelling, dates, inline source citation, controlled vocabularies, the no-recommendation-of-record-before-gate rule, and the copay compliance line, in both deliverables.

Alongside the two deliverables, submit claims.json containing a key_figures object with these exact keys: us_addressable_patients (addressable US GPP patients), blended_first_pass_pa_approval_pct (share-weighted first-pass PA approval across insured lives, as a fraction 0-1), blended_gross_to_net_pct (blended gross-to-net erosion as a fraction 0-1).

deliverables.structured_schema_description: pa_workflow.yaml — a machine-readable workflow spec with these top-level keys: (1) product: an object naming the product and its benefit routing (brand, generic, route_of_administration, benefit_type, medicare_pathway). (2) payer_segments: a list of objects, one per segment (commercial, medicare, medicaid, uninsured), each with fields segment, share_pct, benefit_design, pa_required, expected_first_pass_approval_pct, turnaround_days_standard, turnaround_days_expedited. (3) workflow_steps: a list of at least 12 objects, each with step_id, name, actor, system, inputs, outputs, sla_business_days, failure_paths — covering intake, benefits verification, PA preparation, PA submission, determination, denial handling, appeal levels, specialty-pharmacy fulfillment, bridge/PAP routing, nursing/injection training, and adherence follow-up. (4) appeals: a list of at least 3 level objects (e.g. payer reconsideration/internal appeal, peer-to-peer, external/independent review or Part D redetermination ladder), each with level, name, actor, sla. (5) patient_support: an object with hub_services (list), bridge_program (object incl. duration_days and eligibility), and copay_program (object incl. annual_max_usd, eligible_population, and the legal constraint that federal healthcare program beneficiaries are not eligible) — plus a pap/foundation route for government-insured and uninsured patients. (6) kpis: a list of at least 5 objects, each with kpi, target, rationale. Use the controlled vocabularies from the engagement standards: benefit_design/benefit_type one of 'pharmacy benefit' or 'medical benefit'; PA outcomes 'approved' | 'denied' | 'pended'. Also submit claims.json: {"key_figures": {"us_addressable_patients": <number>, "blended_first_pass_pa_approval_pct": <fraction 0-1>, "blended_gross_to_net_pct": <fraction 0-1>}}.
